sha256:936b6f0f6f9f0fabc7119d5f027af6a48.body:
`count_words(text)` returns the word count the composer shows under a post's text box. Today an empty post says **1 word**, and a double space counts an extra word.

- A word is a run of characters that are not whitespace. Words are separated by any run of whitespace: spaces, tabs, newlines and carriage returns, in any mix and number.
- Whitespace at the start or end adds no words, so an empty or blank post has 0 words.
- Punctuation, digits, symbols and non-English letters are part of the word they are in, and a symbol standing on its own between spaces is a word.

sha256:939c40f234b018d342c21788a45501c2f.body:
Since the cart moved to integer cents, the cart drawer shows amounts the way the API stores them. From a support ticket:

> My cart says the sofa costs **129900**. Is that dollars?? And my refund line says **-500**.

`formatPrice(cents)` in `src/format-price.js` is what the drawer, the receipts and the refund lines use to show an amount. Show dollars with two decimals and comma thousands separators: `123456` → `"$1,234.56"`. Negative amounts are refunds, and the minus goes before the dollar sign, as on the receipts: `-500` → `"-$5.00"`.

sha256:957e830d12003b4cbfb762a654035a7da.body:
The search box sends a request on every keystroke, about eight per query. It should send one request per pause in typing.

`debounceTimes(keystrokes, waitMs)` gets the keystroke times in milliseconds, in order (several can share a time), and the wait in milliseconds (0 or more). Return the times at which a search request fires, in order.

- Each keystroke schedules a request `waitMs` after it.
- A keystroke at or before the time the scheduled request would fire cancels it, and schedules its own.
- No keystrokes, no requests.

Since the cart moved to integer cents, the cart drawer shows amounts the way the API stores them. From a support ticket:

> My cart says the sofa costs **129900**. Is that dollars?? And my refund line says **-500**.

`formatPrice(cents)` takes an amount as a whole number of cents and returns the text the drawer, the receipts and the refund lines show.

- Show a dollar sign, then the whole dollars with a comma between every group of three digits, then a dot and exactly two digits of cents: `123456` → `"$1,234.56"`, `5` → `"$0.05"`.
- Negative amounts are refunds. The minus goes before the dollar sign, as on the receipts: `-500` → `"-$5.00"`.
- Amounts can run into the billions of cents.

Security raised the minimum password length to 12, and the sign-up form says 12, but the API still checks 8 and reports no other rule.

`PasswordPolicy.violations(password)` returns every rule the password breaks, in this order:

1. `"too-short"`: fewer than 12 characters. Every character counts, whitespace included.
2. `"no-digit"`: no digit.
3. `"no-letter"`: no letter, in either case.
4. `"has-whitespace"`: a space, tab or other whitespace character anywhere.

A password that breaks none of them gets an empty list.

sha256:a6568afbb3ad31a8c1edfc0a60f0a00cb.body:
Mateo replaced the response cache's `std::unordered_map` index with an open-addressing table on Thursday (#412, notes in `docs/412-cache-index.md`) to take the per-insert allocation off the hot path. CPU at peak is down 9%, but since the deploy:

- the cache hit ratio went from **94.1%** to **71.3%**, worst on the PoPs that purge the most;
- origin requests are up **3.2×**;
- `edgectl cache get` reports misses for keys whose responses are visibly in the arena.

```text
14:02:11 purge key=3                        ok
14:02:19 get   key=11  miss                 (arena slot 4: key=11, age 41s)
14:02:19 get   key=19  miss                 (arena slot 5: key=19, age 38s)
```

`cache_index(slots, ops)` in `src/cache_index.cpp` replays a cache log against an index of `slots` slots: `["put", key, value]`, `["get", key]` and `["erase", key]` (a purge). It returns what each get found, `-1` for a miss. The index must behave like a map of at most `slots` entries: a get finds the latest value put under its key unless the key was purged since, and a put is refused (the response is served uncached) only when every slot holds a live entry. A purged response must never come back. Keep the flat table: going back to a node-based map is not the fix.

docs/412-cache-index.md.text:
# #412: open-addressing cache index

Author: Mateo O. Merged Thursday, deployed to every PoP by 14:00.

## Why

The response cache's index was a `std::unordered_map<int, int>`: one heap node per insert. At
peak that was 9% of CPU on the edge flame graphs, most of it in `operator new` and `free`.

## What

A flat array of `cache.index_slots` slots, allocated once at startup. A key's home slot is
`key % slots`; on a collision, the next slot, wrapping around at the end (linear probing).
A lookup walks from the home slot until it finds the key or reaches an empty slot. When every
slot holds an entry, a new response is served without being cached.

## Results (canary PoP, 24 h)

- CPU at peak: -9.2%
- p99 time to first byte: 3.1 ms → 2.6 ms
- Allocations per request on the cache path: 1 → 0

sha256:a7d434b1858edc7bc26cd2fbf95f53959.body:
Sign-up compares email addresses exactly as typed, so someone who signed up as `Jane.Doe@Example.com` and signs up again as `jane.doe@example.com ` gets a second account. Write the key sign-up looks accounts up by, so one person gets one account however they type their address. (The address itself is still stored exactly as typed; this is only the lookup key.)

`CanonicalEmail(raw)` returns the key and `ok` true, or `""` and `ok` false for anything that is not an address we accept:

- Surrounding whitespace is ignored. Whitespace anywhere inside the address (spaces, tabs, any Unicode space) makes it invalid.
- An address has exactly one `@`, with something on both sides of it.
- The whole address is lowercased: every provider our users are on treats the local part case-insensitively.
- For **gmail.com** and **googlemail.com** (those exact domains after lowercasing; not their subdomains or longer domains), dots in the local part are dropped, so is everything from the first `+` on, and the domain becomes `gmail.com`. Other domains keep their dots and `+` tags as they are: plenty of mail servers deliver `+` addresses to different people.
- If the Gmail rules leave the local part empty, the address is invalid.

src/gateway/policy.ts.text:
/**
 * Session rules for the login gateway, as signed off by security (SEC-118).
 *
 * A login starts a session family. A client refreshes with the family's current refresh token
 * and gets the next one; each refresh token works once. A refresh is decided in this order:
 *
 *   1. A token that is not in the family: sign in again ("unknown").
 *   2. A revoked family (signed out everywhere, password changed): sign in again ("revoked").
 *   3. A family SESSION_LIFETIME_MS or more after its login: sign in again ("expired").
 *   4. A token that was already rotated:
 *      - up to REFRESH_GRACE_MS after its rotation (inclusive), the client lost a race with
 *        itself: answer with the family's current token and issue nothing new;
 *      - any later, someone else has a copy: sign in again ("reuse") and revoke the family.
 *   5. Otherwise rotate: issue the family's next token.
 *
 * Only "reuse" revokes the family: every token in it stops working, the current one included.
 */

/** Mobile sessions last 30 days from login, however often they refresh. */
export const SESSION_LIFETIME_MS = 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

/** How long a just-rotated token is still answered, for clients that refresh twice at once. */
export const REFRESH_GRACE_MS = 10 * 1000;

sha256:a96ac4ef5192b6fbc6bfaca4c064d4fa6.body:
The season report fails as soon as it reaches the sheets from the Oregon volunteers:

```text
  File "notebook/units.py", line 9, in to_mm
    return float(value) * MM_PER[unit]
KeyError: 'in'
```

Their sheets differ from ours in three ways:

- lengths in inches (`0.6 in`), and sometimes no space or a capital unit (`12mm`, `1.3 CM`, `0.5in`);
- lots nobody measured have the length left blank, or a `?` when the volunteer wasn't sure.

`length_report(lines)` in `notebook/report.py` gives, per species, the number of lots measured and the shortest, longest and mean length in millimetres, each rounded to one decimal. An inch is 25.4 mm. Unmeasured lots don't count towards any of those numbers, but their species still appears: with no measured lot it shows `measured: 0` and `None` for the lengths.

The label printer converts lengths with `to_mm` in `notebook/units.py` too, and it should print the inch lots as well.

notebook/__init__.py.text: """The field notebook: specimen lots typed up from the paper notebook, and what we report on them."""

notebook/labels.py.text:
"""Notebook lines, as typed up from the paper field notebook. One line per specimen lot:

    2026-06-03 | Ridge B | Carabus nemoralis | 14.5 mm | 2

date | site | species | body length | individuals in the lot. The length is left blank when
nothing was measured.
"""

FIELDS = ("date", "site", "species", "length", "count")


def fields(line):
    """The five fields of a line, stripped, as written."""
    parts = [part.strip() for part in line.split("|")]
    if len(parts) != len(FIELDS):
        raise ValueError(f"expected {len(FIELDS)} fields: {line!r}")
    return parts


def parse_line(line):
    """A line as a dict: every field as written, the count as a number."""
    row = dict(zip(FIELDS, fields(line)))
    row["count"] = int(row["count"])
    return row

notebook/units.py.text:
"""Lengths as written in the notebook, converted to millimetres. The label printer uses
to_mm too."""

MM_PER = {"mm": 1, "cm": 10}


def to_mm(text):
    """'14.5 mm' or '1.2 cm' in millimetres."""
    value, unit = text.split()
    return float(value) * MM_PER[unit]

sha256:a974f21dbee52f39bbc8bcb1f0e8640d1.body:
Some subscribers got last week's newsletter three times. The sync sends one email per customer record, and the CRM export has several records for the same person:

```text
id  email
1   Ann@x.io
2    ann@x.io
3   bo@x.io
```

`dedupe(records)` runs before the newsletter sync. It gets a list of customer records, dicts with at least an `id` and an `email`, and returns the list without duplicates.

- Two records are duplicates when their emails match ignoring letter case (any letter, not only ASCII) and spaces around them. Only the email decides; ids and other fields don't.
- Keep the first record for each email and drop the later ones. Records stay in their original order.
- A kept record is passed on unchanged, every field included: the sync and the CRM both need the email as it was written.

dedupe.py.text:
def dedupe(records):
    """Keep the first record for each email before the newsletter sync.

    Emails compare case-insensitively, ignoring surrounding spaces. Order is kept.
    """
    return records

# Data platform

Partners drop CSV exports in a bucket every night. A pipeline cleans them, loads the warehouse and feeds the reports finance reads on Monday morning.

The exports are messier than anyone admits: quoted commas in company names, duplicate customers with slightly different emails, and orders that never got paid. When the numbers look wrong, this is where people come asking.

## What you'll work on

- Parsing awkward input files without losing data
- Cleaning and deduplicating records before they reach the warehouse
- SQL for the reports and reconciliations people rely on

## Good fit if you

- Work with data, or are the person on your team who ends up writing the SQL
- Enjoy turning messy input into something you can trust
- Know **Python**, **SQL** or **C#**, or want more practice with them

Stack: Python, SQL, and C# for the billing jobs.

sha256:a982b8493dfae753a5c4c84f45ecd7bbd.body:
`WordCount.Count(text)` returns the word count the composer shows under a post's text box. Today an empty post says **1 word**, and a double space counts an extra word.

- A word is a run of characters that are not whitespace. Words are separated by any run of whitespace: spaces, tabs, newlines and carriage returns, in any mix and number.
- Whitespace at the start or end adds no words, so an empty or blank post has 0 words.
- Punctuation, digits, symbols and non-English letters are part of the word they are in, and a symbol standing on its own between spaces is a word.

sha256:b1f7cc85001b661f49b4888f905aaba89.body:
Monday's import into the herbarium database created 14 "new" species that we already had. From the import log:

```text
new species: Carabus Nemoralis        (have: Carabus nemoralis)
new species: Carabus Sp.              (have: Carabus sp.)
new species: Pterostichus Niger       (have: Pterostichus niger)
```

`species_tally(lines)` in `notebook/tally.py` totals individuals per species for the end-of-day tally sheet, and the sheet is what gets imported. It still has its own `_clean` from before `notebook/names.py` existed, and the two have drifted apart. The tally should key every species by `canonical_name`, the way the herbarium files it, and `_clean` should go. Blank lines are skipped, as now.

notebook/__init__.py.text: """The field notebook: specimen lots typed up from the paper notebook, and what we report on them."""

notebook/labels.py.text:
"""Notebook lines, as typed up from the paper field notebook. One line per specimen lot:

    2026-06-03 | Ridge B | Carabus nemoralis | 14.5 mm | 2

date | site | species | body length | individuals in the lot. The length is left blank when
nothing was measured.
"""

FIELDS = ("date", "site", "species", "length", "count")


def fields(line):
    """The five fields of a line, stripped, as written."""
    parts = [part.strip() for part in line.split("|")]
    if len(parts) != len(FIELDS):
        raise ValueError(f"expected {len(FIELDS)} fields: {line!r}")
    return parts


def parse_line(line):
    """A line as a dict: every field as written, the count as a number."""
    row = dict(zip(FIELDS, fields(line)))
    row["count"] = int(row["count"])
    return row

## What you'll work on

- Formatting money and other values the way customers expect to read them
- Form behaviour, validation and accessible markup
- Small performance fixes in the browser, like debouncing input

## Good fit if you

- Build user interfaces, or want to get sharper at the details that make one feel solid

sha256:b6c151c3f9ec3fe33713a0be00af54b0a.body:
The cart drawer and the header badge show whatever `Cart.summary()` returns. To keep the drawer fast, `summary()` was memoised: the drawer calls it on every render, and repricing a 60-line cart each time cost 38 ms a frame (now about 2). Since then the drawer sometimes shows an old total. A shopper's report:

> I changed the jeans from 1 to 2 in my cart and it still said $59.00. Then checkout charged me $118.00.

Removing an item shows the right total; changing a quantity doesn't. Make every `summary()` reflect the cart as it is at that moment, and keep the memo.

**What `summary()` returns.** `{ items, subtotal, discount, total }`, amounts in whole cents: `items` is the sum of the lines' quantities, `subtotal` the sum of `price × quantity`, `discount` the promo code's discount on the subtotal, and `total` is `subtotal − discount`.

**The cart.**

- `add(sku, price, quantity = 1)` adds that quantity to the line with that SKU, or adds a new line `{ sku, price, quantity }` if there is none. Adding to an existing line keeps the line's price.
- `setQuantity(sku, quantity)` sets a line's quantity; 0 or less removes the line. It does nothing for a SKU not in the cart.
- `remove(sku)` removes the line.
- `applyCode(code)` sets the promo code: `{ name, percent }`, `{ name, amount }` (in cents), or `null` to remove it. Two codes can share a name and differ in what they take off.

**Discounts.** `discountFor(code, subtotal)`, imported from `./discounts.js`, is 0 without a code; a percent code takes `Math.round(subtotal × percent / 100)`, an amount code takes its amount, and the discount is never more than the subtotal. `sum(amounts)`, imported from `./money.js`, adds up an array of numbers.

**The memo stays.** `summary()` must not reprice the cart when nothing changed since the last call. Keep the result cached in a field on the cart named for what it does (the starter's `this.cache`, or for example a version number or a dirty flag) rather than taking the memo out.

**Tests.** `replay(actions)` plays a session on a new cart and returns what `summary()` showed each time it was asked. Actions are `["add", sku, price, quantity?]`, `["quantity", sku, quantity]`, `["remove", sku]`, `["code", code]` and `["summary"]`.

The category page's filter form has two checkboxes, `in-stock` and `on-sale`, with bare text next to them. The accessibility audit flagged them: screen readers announce "checkbox" and nothing else, and clicking the text does not toggle the box.

Tie each checkbox to a label:

sha256:bd006e88cb3949b9547fede56f9f60031.body:
Rui escalated Bluefin's October reconciliation:

> Bluefin's statement for 3 October says we're owed **€59.50** on 2 orders. Our settlement report says **€75.00** with **2 rejected rows**. Every night since 1 October has had rejected rows, always Bluefin's. Northwind still matches to the cent.

Bluefin's partner note from 28 September:

> From 1 October our settlement exports write negative amounts in accounting format: refunds and fees appear in brackets, e.g. `(12.50)`.

Their file for 3 October:

```text
partner,order_id,type,amount,currency
Bluefin,BF-77101,sale,45.00,EUR
Bluefin,BF-77102,sale,30.00,EUR
Bluefin,BF-77101,refund,(12.50),EUR
Bluefin,BF-FEE-10,adjustment,(3.00),EUR
```

`settlement_summary(text)` in `pipeline/report.py` is what finance reconciles against: per partner and currency, the number of sales and refunds and the net in cents, plus how many rows were rejected. Net is sales less refunds, plus adjustments with their own sign. A refund always reduces net by its amount, whichever way a partner writes it: Northwind writes refunds as positive amounts. `read_settlements` in `pipeline/readers.py` also loads `raw_settlements` in the warehouse, so its rows keep amounts signed as the partner wrote them. A row that still can't be read is rejected and counted, not guessed at.

pipeline/__init__.py.text: """Nightly settlement pipeline: read partner exports, load the warehouse, report to finance."""

pipeline/readers.py.text:
import csv
import io

from pipeline.money import to_cents

KINDS = {"sale", "refund", "adjustment"}


def read_settlements(text):
    """The rows of a partner settlement export, and how many rows were rejected.

    Each row has partner, order, kind, currency and amount: signed cents, as the partner
    wrote them. These rows are also loaded into raw_settlements as they are. A row that can't
    be read is rejected (counted and left out) rather than guessed at.
    """
    rows = []
    rejected = 0
    for raw in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text)):
        kind = raw["type"].strip().lower()
        if kind not in KINDS:
            rejected += 1
            continue
        try:
            amount = to_cents(raw["amount"])
        except ValueError:
            rejected += 1
            continue
        rows.append({
            "partner": raw["partner"].strip(),
            "order": raw["order_id"].strip(),
            "kind": kind,
            "currency": raw["currency"].strip().upper(),
            "amount": amount,
        })
    return rows, rejected

Since Northwind started quoting company names, their nightly customer import loads rows into the wrong columns. From last night's load:

```text
line   "Acme, Inc.",42,"NY"
loaded name='"Acme'  account=' Inc."'  region='42'
```

`parse_csv_line(line)` in `parse_csv_line.py` splits one line of a partner export into its fields. Fields are separated by commas, except inside double quotes. The quotes around a field are not part of it, and a doubled quote inside a quoted field is a literal quote: `"say ""hi"""` → `say "hi"`. A quoted field may contain a line break. Spaces are kept as written, and an empty line is a single empty field, which the import reports as a row with no name.

"""Normalising fields before records are compared or loaded."""


def normalize_email(email):
    """An email as we compare it: trimmed and lowercased.

    None when there is no usable email on file (missing, empty or only spaces): phone and
    in-store customers often have none.

    if email is None:
        return None
    email = email.strip().lower()
    return email or None

sha256:ceedbc83457228a414f3e26e047974d5f.body:
The edge proxy keeps the most recent request latencies in memory, in a fixed-size ring buffer that overwrites its oldest entry when it is full.

`ring_buffer(capacity, values, count, out)` pushes the `count` integers in `values`, in order, into an empty buffer that holds `capacity` entries. A push into a full buffer overwrites the oldest entry. Then it writes what the buffer holds into `out`, oldest first, and returns how many entries it wrote.

- `out` has room for at least `count` integers.
- A capacity of 0 holds nothing.
- This runs on the hot path: don't allocate memory (no `malloc`).

Customers type promo codes the way they read them in the email, and checkout rejects codes typed in lowercase or with stray spaces.

`applyDiscount(totalCents, code, codes)` returns an order's total after its promo code's discount.

- `totalCents` is the total in whole cents. `code` is what the customer typed. `codes` maps each configured code to its percent off, from 0 to 100: `{ SAVE10: 10 }`.
- The typed code matches a configured code when the two are equal ignoring letter case and ignoring spaces before and after the typed code. Spaces inside a code still count, and configured codes may be written in any case. Only codes in `codes` match.
- With a match, return the total less that percentage, rounded down to whole cents.
- Without a match, including an empty or blank code, return the total unchanged.

sha256:d52b73c22792aa51915c11af8d6ef64c2.body:
Finance's September sales-tax filing came out $310.22 under the tax customers were actually charged. The filing is the sum of what `lineTaxes` returns for every order, and those line taxes don't add up to the order's tax. A receipt also charged tax on a gift card.

One order, at 8.25%, as the receipt shows it today:

```text
Order #20417                      net      tax
  Rain jacket                  $45.00    $3.71
  Tee × 2                      $45.00    $3.71
  Socks                        $10.80    $0.89
  Tax                                    $8.32   ← the lines add up to $8.31
```

Fix `receipt(order)` and `lineTaxes(amounts, rate)` so they follow Finance's rules. All amounts are whole cents; rates are basis points (825 is 8.25%).

**Input.** An `Order` is `{ id, taxRate, lines }`. Each line is `{ sku, price, quantity, discount, taxable }`: `price` is per unit, `discount` is the line's share of the order's promo code, and `taxable` is `false` for gift cards and donations.

**Output.** A `Receipt` is `{ lines, net, tax, total }`, where `lines` has one `{ sku, net, tax }` per order line, in order.

**Rules.**

- A line's `net` is `price × quantity − discount`. The receipt's `net` is the sum of every line's net, gift cards included.
- A line's taxable amount is its net when `taxable` is `true`, and 0 when it is `false`. A non-taxable line's tax is 0.
- The order is taxed once: the sum of the taxable amounts times the rate, divided by 10,000 and rounded half up to the cent. That is the receipt's `tax`, and `total` is `net + tax`.
- The line taxes add up to exactly the order's tax. Each line first gets its taxable amount times the rate, divided by 10,000 and rounded down. The cents still missing go one each to the lines with the largest remainders from that division; on a tie, the earlier line gets the cent first.
- `lineTaxes(amounts, rate)` takes the lines' taxable amounts in order and returns each line's tax by the rule above. Keep it exported with that signature (the finance export calls it with the taxable amounts) and take the receipt's line taxes from it.
- Keep money in whole cents: no `toFixed` or `parseFloat`.

`taxOn(amount, rate)` in the file is the tax on one amount, rounded half up to the cent.

A credential-stuffing bot hit the login endpoint again last night. Limit login attempts with a sliding window.

`allow(times, limit, windowMs)` gets the times of login attempts in milliseconds, in order (several can share a time), and returns, for each attempt, whether it is allowed.

- An attempt at time `t` is allowed when fewer than `limit` allowed attempts fall in the window from just after `t − windowMs` up to and including `t`. Otherwise it is rejected.
- Rejected attempts don't count toward the limit.
- `limit` can be 0, which rejects every attempt.

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

/**
 * Whether a password reset link has expired. Timestamps are Unix seconds;
 * a link stays valid until $issuedAt + $ttlMinutes * 60, inclusive.
 */
function isExpired(int $issuedAt, int $now, int $ttlMinutes): bool
{

Rui sent this after reconciling September:

> The collected-by-partner report says Northwind paid us **$1,284.00** in September. Their remittances add up to **$942.00**. And Corvid isn't on the report at all. They're the one I need to chase: they haven't paid a cent since August.

Northwind moved its bigger customers onto two-part invoices in August, so some orders now have more than one payment, and some are only partly paid so far.

Fix the collected-by-partner query. It reads two tables:

| Table | Column | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `orders` | `id` | `integer`, primary key | the order |
| `orders` | `partner` | `text`, not null | the partner the order came through |
| `orders` | `total` | `numeric(12, 2)`, not null | what the order was invoiced for |
| `payments` | `id` | `integer`, primary key | the payment |
| `payments` | `order_id` | `integer`, not null, references `orders (id)` | the order it pays for |
| `payments` | `amount` | `numeric(12, 2)`, not null | the amount received |

An order can have no payments, one, or several, and its payments need not add up to its total.

The query returns one row per partner that has at least one order, with two columns:

1. `partner`;
2. `collected`: the sum of every payment received on that partner's orders, or `0` when none of them has been paid.

Rows are ordered by `collected`, biggest first; partners with the same amount are in alphabetical order, so the PDF doesn't reshuffle every month. With no orders the result has no rows.

Requirement: every payment counts. Two payments of the same amount are two payments, so don't add up only the distinct amounts.

-- Finance's collected-by-partner report: what each partner's customers have paid us.
-- orders(id, partner, total), payments(id, order_id, amount)
SELECT o.partner, SUM(o.total) AS collected
FROM orders o
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.partner
ORDER BY collected DESC;

sha256:e2cafd032130cebd050088cccdf3e6dac.body:
Since the IPv6 listener went live on Tuesday, every request that addresses the proxy by its v6 literal gets the default vhost's **421 Misdirected Request**. The health checker on `[2001:db8::1]:8080` has been red since; on-call silenced it at 02:10.

```text
421 GET http://[2001:db8::1]:8080/healthz host="[2001" vhost=default
421 GET http://[2001:db8::1]/healthz      host="["     vhost=default
```

The proxy routes each request on its Host header after `normalize_host` has normalized it, and the response cache keys on the same value, so two spellings of one host share a vhost and cache entries. Plain hostnames already work; IPv6 literals do not, because the current code treats the first `:` as the start of the port.

## What to write

`int normalize_host(const char *host, char *out, size_t size)`

- `host` is the raw Host header value, a NUL-terminated string.
- Write the normalized host into `out`, NUL-terminated, and return its length (not counting the terminator).
- `size` is the size of `out` in bytes, terminator included. If the result plus its terminator does not fit, return `-1`.
- Return `-1` when the value is not a host. The examples show `-1` as `null`, and a string for a host.

## Normalizing rules

- **Port:** remove the port. For a hostname, the port is everything from the first `:` on (`example.com:8443` becomes `example.com`).
- **IPv6 literals:** a value starting with `[` is an IPv6 literal. It keeps its brackets and loses only a port after the closing `]` (`[2001:db8::1]:8080` becomes `[2001:db8::1]`). A literal that is never closed with `]`, or whose `]` is followed by anything other than nothing or a `:` port, is not a host.
- **Trailing dot:** after the port is removed, a single trailing `.` is removed (`cdn.example.com.` becomes `cdn.example.com`).
- **Case:** ASCII letters are lowercased, in hostnames and IPv6 literals alike (`Example.COM` becomes `example.com`).
- **Empty:** a value with nothing left after these steps is not a host.

Plain hostnames must keep normalizing exactly as they do now.

## Constraints

- No heap allocation: `normalize_host` runs on every request before routing, and `out` is the buffer to write into. Do not call `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, `strdup` or `strndup`.

use PHPUnit\Framework\Attributes\DataProvider;
use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase;

// Acceptance criteria for QUICK-8. CI runs these cases and 14 more it does not show.
final class CountWordsTest extends TestCase
{
    /** [arguments, expected] as JSON. */
    public static function cases(): array
    {
        return [
            'case 1' => ['""', '0'],
            'case 2' => ['"hello world"', '2'],
            'case 3' => ['"  spaced   out  "', '2'],
            'case 4' => ['"one"', '1'],
            'case 5' => ['"   "', '0'],
        ];
    }

    #[DataProvider('cases')]
    public function testCountWords(string $input, string $expected): void
    {
        $args = json_decode($input, true);
        $actual = countWords($args);
        $this->assertSame(json_decode($expected, true), $actual);
    }
}

**SEV-1 · checkout-api · paged 02:14**

> **checkout-api: 5xx rate 58% (threshold 2%) for 9 minutes.** `POST /quote` is failing.

You're on call for Kettlebrook, a homeware shop. Checkout is failing for a lot of customers, and tonight the team's AI tools are down as well: the coding assistant, the log summariser and the bot that writes status updates. It's you, the logs and the tests. The rest of the team is in the chat.

**Restore checkout**

1. Find what's failing in `logs/checkout-api.log`.
2. Reproduce it. The failing order from the logs is already a regression test in `src/checkout/quote.test.js`: run the tests (Ctrl/⌘-Enter).
3. Fix it in `src/checkout/quote.js`, `src/checkout/shipping.js` or both, so every order gets a correct quote: guests and members, with free shipping where it applies.
4. Open a pull request, get CI green and merge it. Main goes straight to production.

`quoteOrder(order)` returns `{ subtotal, shipping, total }` in cents. Shipping is $4.95. It's free from $50 for everyone, and from $30 for loyalty members (CHK-412, shipped Thursday). README.md.text:
# Incident: checkout is down

Kettlebrook sells mugs, linen and candles to people who really want their mugs. `checkout-api` prices every basket: `POST /quote` turns a basket into a subtotal, shipping and a total, and the payment page charges exactly that.

The team leans on AI tools for most of its day. Tonight those tools are down, and so is checkout.

- `src/checkout/quote.js`: the quote.
- `src/checkout/shipping.js`: shipping and its thresholds.
- `src/checkout/money.js`: money helpers (read-only).
- `logs/checkout-api.log`: the last few minutes of production logs.
- `RUNBOOK.md`: what to do when paged.

RUNBOOK.md.text:
# checkout-api on-call runbook

_Last reviewed: when the assistant was up._

1. Paste the alert into the assistant.
2. Do what it says.
3. If the assistant is unavailable, see step 1.

## Appendix B (recovered from the 2019 wiki export)

- Read the logs: `logs/checkout-api.log`. The stack trace names a file and a line.
- Reproduce it with a test before changing anything. Run tests: Ctrl/⌘-Enter.
- Fix it, open a pull request (Ctrl/⌘-Shift-Enter), wait for CI, merge it. Main ships itself.
- Don't wrap it in a try/catch and go back to bed. We will find out.

text: Traffic jumped at 02:00 when the "Midnight mugs" newsletter went out. Most of those visitors check out as guests.
Every complaint tonight is from someone checking out without an account. Members aren't writing in.
CHK-412 is mine, shipped Thursday: members get free shipping from $30. The member check is in `quote.js`, the thresholds in `shipping.js`. I tested it with my own account, which is a member account.
A catch here turns the crash into a silently wrong quote. Handle the guest case explicitly instead of catching the error.
Nit: these amounts are defined in `shipping.js`. Import the constants so the thresholds live in one place.

chat.text: I'm on comms, you're on the fix. The status bot is down too, so tonight's updates are artisanal.
Support queue is at 212. One customer has written MY MUGS four times, which is fair.
The newsletter was mine. "No account needed!" felt like a great headline at 6pm.
Reading logs by hand at 2am. Respect.
Is that red test my change? Please say it isn't my change.
Green locally? Status page draft: "We've identified the issue." First update I've typed myself in years, and it's true.
I'll tell the queue the moment it's merged. No pressure. Some pressure.
Finance, awake for reasons. Guests pay shipping under $50 again on that build. I have never been this happy to see a fee.
Merged and shipping. Marking it resolved on the status page, by hand, slowly, savouring it.
Telling the queue now. Someone already replied MY MUGS!! but happier.
Next newsletter headline: "Checkout works." Bold, I know.

A guest has no loyalty record at all, and a lapsed member's tier is "none". Read your membership check out loud for both: does it call either of them a member?

# Weighted balancing

Status: agreed, for the origin-v2 canary. Owner: Mateo.

`server <name> weight=<n>;` gives a server n shares of an upstream's requests. `weight=0`
drains it: it keeps its place in the block but gets no requests. An upstream whose servers
are all drained has nowhere to send a request.

## Smooth, not bursty

With 5:1:1 a naive scheme sends five requests in a row to the first server. We do what nginx
does instead, so the small server's requests are spread out:

1. Every server starts with a current value of 0.
2. For each request, add each server's weight to its current value.
3. Pick the server with the highest current value; on a tie, the one listed first.
4. Subtract the total weight of all servers that took part from the picked server's value.

Drained servers take part in nothing: their weight is not added and does not count towards
the total.

## Worked example: a=5, b=1, c=1

| Request | After adding weights (a, b, c) | Picked | After subtracting 7 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5, 1, 1 | a | -2, 1, 1 |
| 2 | 3, 2, 2 | a | -4, 2, 2 |
| 3 | 1, 3, 3 | b | 1, -4, 3 |
| 4 | 6, -3, 4 | a | -1, -3, 4 |
| 5 | 4, -2, 5 | c | 4, -2, -2 |
| 6 | 9, -1, -1 | a | 2, -1, -1 |
| 7 | 7, 0, 0 | a | 0, 0, 0 |

After seven requests every value is back at 0 and the cycle repeats: a a b a c a a.

# Edge proxy

A small proxy in front of everything: it terminates connections, caches hot responses and exports latency metrics. The hot path is C and C++; the control plane and metrics are Go.

Every allocation shows up on a flame graph here. The backlog is about doing more with fixed memory, measuring the right thing, and keeping configuration readable for whoever is paged.

## What you'll work on

- Fixed-size data structures such as ring buffers and LRU caches
- Latency percentiles and the metrics behind dashboards
- Small, strict configuration formats

## Good fit if you

- Do systems or performance work, or want to get closer to the metal
- Think about memory, ordering and what happens under load
- Know **C**, **C++** or **Go**, or are learning one of them

Stack: C, C++, Go.

text: Weights are parsed into `Backend.Weight` already; config isn't the problem. I'd like `edgectl upstream preview` to show the real order before we flip the canary on.
If origin-v2 misbehaves I'll drain it with weight=0 rather than editing the block, so that has to work too.
`Next` runs on every connection's goroutine, and now it reads and writes the counters on each call. Without the lock two requests race on them. Can we keep it?
The lock went missing from `Next`. Every connection goroutine calls it and it updates shared counters, so the race detector will flag this on the first load test.
Nit: `Next` is getting long for something on the request path. Is all of it needed?
That's the 9:1 we want. I'll roll it to one PoP first and watch origin-v2's error rate.

hints.text: Plain round robin only remembers whose turn it is. With weights, each server also has to remember how far ahead of or behind its share it is.
Walk the 5:1:1 table in the design note against your code one request at a time. A drained server should play no part in any of the sums.

Write `shippingBanner(order)`: the text of the banner above the checkout button in the cart drawer, telling the shopper how far the cart is from free shipping, or `null` when there is no banner.

**Input.** An order is `{ code, lines }`. Each line is `{ sku, price, quantity }`, with `price` per unit in whole cents. `code` is the promo code: `null`, a percentage (`{ percent: 10 }`) or a fixed amount in cents (`{ amount: 500 }`).

**Output.** Use this copy exactly:

| Cart | Banner |
|---|---|
| no lines | `null` |
| total under $50.00 | `Spend $12.50 more for free shipping` (the amount still missing) |
| total of $50.00 or more | `Your order ships free` |

**Rules.**

- The total is what checkout charges for the lines after the promo code, the same total `shippingFor(order)` in the file compares with `FREE_SHIPPING_FROM` (5000 cents). The banner must never promise free shipping that checkout then charges for, or ask for more when checkout already ships free.
- A cart is empty only when it has no lines. A cart with lines whose total is $0.00 still shows how much more to spend.
- Amounts read as everywhere else in the cart: a dollar sign, whole dollars with commas between thousands, a dot and two digits of cents, as in `$1,234.56` and `$0.05`.

**Code you can use.**

- `orderTotal(order)`, already imported from `./totals.js`, returns the total in cents: the sum of `price × quantity` over the lines, less the code's discount. A percentage code takes `Math.round(subtotal × percent / 100)` off; an amount code takes its amount off; either way the discount is never more than the subtotal, so the total is never below 0.
- `formatPrice(cents)` from `./format.js` (`import { formatPrice } from "./format.js";`) formats cents as above: `formatPrice(123456)` is `"$1,234.56"`.

# Shop

The online shop customers actually see: product listings, filters, the cart and a three-step checkout. Pages are server-rendered, with a thin layer of TypeScript for the interactive parts.

Conversion dipped after the last redesign. Support is fielding tickets about prices, promo codes and a search box that feels sluggish, and an accessibility audit came back with a long list.

## What you'll work on

- Formatting money and other values the way customers expect to read them
- Form behaviour, validation and accessible markup
- Small performance fixes in the browser, like debouncing input

## Good fit if you

- Build user interfaces, or want to get sharper at the details that make one feel solid
- Are comfortable with **JavaScript**, **TypeScript** or plain **HTML**
- Care what a bug looks like from the customer's side of the screen

Stack: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML.

# Data platform

Partners drop CSV exports in a bucket every night. A pipeline cleans them, loads the warehouse and feeds the reports finance reads on Monday morning.

The exports are messier than anyone admits: quoted commas in company names, duplicate customers with slightly different emails, and orders that never got paid. When the numbers look wrong, this is where people come asking.

## What you'll work on

- Parsing awkward input files without losing data
- Cleaning and deduplicating records before they reach the warehouse
- SQL for the reports and reconciliations people rely on

## Good fit if you

- Work with data, or are the person on your team who ends up writing the SQL
- Enjoy turning messy input into something you can trust
- Know **Python**, **SQL** or **C#**, or want more practice with them

Stack: Python, SQL, and C# for the billing jobs.

Ada's PR #812 memoised `Cart.summary()` last Thursday. The cart drawer calls it on every render, and on a 60-line cart that was costing 38 ms a frame; now it's about 2. Since the release, support has a stack of tickets like this one:

> I changed the jeans from 1 to 2 in my cart and it still said $59.00. Then checkout charged me $118.00.

Checkout prices the order on the server, so nobody was overcharged, but the drawer and the header badge show whatever `summary()` in `src/cart/cart.js` returns. Find what the memo broke and fix it. Keep the memo.

`replay(actions)` at the bottom of the file is what the cart's tests use: it plays a session on a new cart and returns what `summary()` showed each time it was asked.

# Shop

The online shop customers actually see: product listings, filters, the cart and a three-step checkout. Pages are server-rendered, with a thin layer of TypeScript for the interactive parts.

Conversion dipped after the last redesign. Support is fielding tickets about prices, promo codes and a search box that feels sluggish, and an accessibility audit came back with a long list.

## What you'll work on

- Formatting money and other values the way customers expect to read them
- Form behaviour, validation and accessible markup
- Small performance fixes in the browser, like debouncing input

## Good fit if you

- Build user interfaces, or want to get sharper at the details that make one feel solid
- Are comfortable with **JavaScript**, **TypeScript** or plain **HTML**
- Care what a bug looks like from the customer's side of the screen

Stack: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML.

sha256:f9fdd679d880b75cb995eb21b9d405f46.body:
Customers keep emailing about a one-cent difference between the invoice and the reminder: the late fee doesn't round the way finance's spreadsheet does.

`LateFee(balance, daysLate)` returns the late fee on an overdue invoice. `balance` is the amount owed in dollars (0 or more, to the cent), and the fee is in dollars too.

- The fee is 0.5% of the balance for each day late, at most 10% of the balance.
- That fee is rounded to cents with halves rounded away from zero, as the spreadsheet does: a fee of 0.505 is 0.51.
- Nothing is charged when `daysLate` is 0 or negative.

sha256:fa160ce08d0e1d90ef65bdafb1809d934.body:
`countWords($text)` returns the word count the composer shows under a post's text box. Today an empty post says **1 word**, and a double space counts an extra word.

- A word is a run of characters that are not whitespace. Words are separated by any run of whitespace: spaces, tabs, newlines and carriage returns, in any mix and number.
- Whitespace at the start or end adds no words, so an empty or blank post has 0 words.
- Punctuation, digits, symbols and non-English letters are part of the word they are in, and a symbol standing on its own between spaces is a word.

# Quick fixes

Small bugs the writing app's team never got round to. Each takes about five minutes, which makes it the five-minute test at /play: pick a language, fix it, merge it.

src/countWords.php.text:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

/** The number of words in a post, as the composer shows it under the text box. */
function countWords(string $text): int
{
    return substr_count($text, " ") + 1;
}

tests/CountWordsTest.php.text:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

use PHPUnit\Framework\Attributes\DataProvider;
use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase;

// Acceptance criteria for QUICK-8. CI runs these cases and 14 more it does not show.
final class CountWordsTest extends TestCase
{
    /** [arguments, expected] as JSON. */
    public static function cases(): array
    {
        return [
            'case 1' => ['""', '0'],
            'case 2' => ['"hello world"', '2'],
            'case 3' => ['"  spaced   out  "', '2'],
            'case 4' => ['"one"', '1'],
            'case 5' => ['"   "', '0'],
        ];
    }

    #[DataProvider('cases')]
    public function testCountWords(string $input, string $expected): void
    {
        $args = json_decode($input, true);
        $actual = countWords($args);
        $this->assertSame(json_decode($expected, true), $actual);

# Edge proxy

A small proxy in front of everything: it terminates connections, caches hot responses and exports latency metrics. The hot path is C and C++; the control plane and metrics are Go.

Every allocation shows up on a flame graph here. The backlog is about doing more with fixed memory, measuring the right thing, and keeping configuration readable for whoever is paged.

## What you'll work on

- Fixed-size data structures such as ring buffers and LRU caches
- Latency percentiles and the metrics behind dashboards
- Small, strict configuration formats

## Good fit if you

- Do systems or performance work, or want to get closer to the metal
- Think about memory, ordering and what happens under load
- Know **C**, **C++** or **Go**, or are learning one of them

Stack: C, C++, Go.

sha256:ff9c83ee33b8219c7030f71b06ad5c7e8.body: `slugify(name)` turns a workspace name into its URL slug: lowercase ASCII letters and digits, with every run of anything else between words becoming a single hyphen, and no hyphen at either end. Accented Latin letters lose their accents first, so `"Café Ünïcorn"` becomes `"cafe-unicorn"`.

lib/slugify.rb.text:
# Workspace URLs are /w/<slug>. Turn a workspace name into its slug:
# lowercase ASCII letters and digits, words joined by single hyphens.
def slugify(name)
  name.downcase.tr(" ", "-")
end

README.md.text:
# Accounts API

The service every client talks to for sign-up, login, sessions and password resets. Most of it is Go, a few older endpoints are still PHP, the admin back office is a small Ruby app, the password service is Java, and the login gateway in front is TypeScript.

It mostly works, and the on-call channel has opinions about the rest: list endpoints that accept any page size, reset links that expire too soon, and logs that are hard to search during an incident.

## What you'll work on

- Parsing and validating request parameters with sensible defaults
- Time and expiry logic, where off-by-one and unit mix-ups hide
- Rate limiting and log handling for the people on call

## Good fit if you

- Write backend services, or want practice with the bugs they actually get
- Like **input validation**, edge cases and reading a stack trace at 2am
- Know **Go**, **PHP**, **Ruby**, **Java** or **TypeScript**, or want to try one of them on familiar problems

Stack: Go, PHP, Ruby, Java, TypeScript.

spec/slugify_spec.rb.text:
# Acceptance criteria for API-5. CI runs these cases and 16 more it does not show.
require "json"
require_relative "../lib/slugify"

RSpec.describe "slugify" do
  # Input and expected output as JSON.
  [
    ["\"Acme Inc\"", "\"acme-inc\""],
    ["\"  Café   Ünïcorn  \"", "\"cafe-unicorn\""],
    ["\"R&D / Ops\"", "\"r-d-ops\""],
    ["\"2024 Planning!!\"", "\"2024-planning\""],
    ["\"---\"", "\"\""],
  ].each_with_index do |(input, expected), i|
    it "passes case #{i + 1}" do
      expect(slugify(JSON.parse(input))).to eq(JSON.parse(expected))
    end
  end
end

sha256:ffb2b4bc3f78ae68b404bfb76f4e4d461.body:
Jo forwarded this from the help desk:

> I got locked out after a few wrong passwords and the page said **"Too many attempts. Try again in 0 minutes."** So I tried again straight away, and it locked me out again.

`retryMessage($secondsLeft)` in `src/retryMessage.php` writes the message the login form shows during a lockout. Lockouts run from one minute up to 24 hours.

- Round the time left **up**, so nobody is told to come back before the lock ends.
- Under 60 minutes (after rounding), say minutes: `Too many attempts. Try again in 1 minute.`, `Too many attempts. Try again in 15 minutes.`
- From 60 minutes on, say hours, also rounded up: `Too many attempts. Try again in 1 hour.`, `Too many attempts. Try again in 2 hours.`
- The lock can end between the check and the page render, so the seconds left can be zero or negative. Then the form says `You can try again now.`

README.md.text:
# Accounts API

The service every client talks to for sign-up, login, sessions and password resets. Most of it is Go, a few older endpoints are still PHP, the admin back office is a small Ruby app, the password service is Java, and the login gateway in front is TypeScript.

It mostly works, and the on-call channel has opinions about the rest: list endpoints that accept any page size, reset links that expire too soon, and logs that are hard to search during an incident.

## What you'll work on

- Parsing and validating request parameters with sensible defaults
- Time and expiry logic, where off-by-one and unit mix-ups hide
- Rate limiting and log handling for the people on call

## Good fit if you

- Write backend services, or want practice with the bugs they actually get
- Like **input validation**, edge cases and reading a stack trace at 2am
- Know **Go**, **PHP**, **Ruby**, **Java** or **TypeScript**, or want to try one of them on familiar problems

Stack: Go, PHP, Ruby, Java, TypeScript.

src/retryMessage.php.text:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

/**
 * The message the login form shows while an account is locked out, for the seconds left on
 * the lock. Lockouts run from one minute up to 24 hours.
 */
function retryMessage(int $secondsLeft): string
{
    $minutes = intdiv($secondsLeft, 60);
    return "Too many attempts. Try again in {$minutes} minutes.";
}

tests/RetryMessageTest.php.text:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

use PHPUnit\Framework\Attributes\DataProvider;
use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase;

// Acceptance criteria for API-7. CI runs these cases and 13 more it does not show.
final class RetryMessageTest extends TestCase
{
    /** [arguments, expected] as JSON. */
    public static function cases(): array
    {
        return [
            'case 1' => ['30', '"Too many attempts. Try again in 1 minute."'],
            'case 2' => ['900', '"Too many attempts. Try again in 15 minutes."'],
            'case 3' => ['61', '"Too many attempts. Try again in 2 minutes."'],
            'case 4' => ['0', '"You can try again now."'],
            'case 5' => ['3600', '"Too many attempts. Try again in 1 hour."'],
        ];
    }

    #[DataProvider('cases')]
    public function testRetryMessage(string $input, string $expected): void
    {
        $args = json_decode($input, true);
        $actual = retryMessage($args);
        $this->assertSame(json_decode($expected, true), $actual);
    }
}

text: Eleven tickets this week with a screenshot of "0 minutes". Most of them locked themselves out twice.
Rounding down is how we got "0 minutes" in the first place. If this rounds, can it round up?
This still rounds down somewhere. Anything that rounds down here tells someone to come back before the lock ends.
Tried the preview with 30 seconds left: "1 minute". That's the one I'll quote back to people.

hints.text: Work out by hand what the form should say with 59 minutes and 1 second left. Does it read as minutes or as hours?
Integer division drops the remainder, and the remainder is exactly the time people are being told they don't have to wait.
